content: Food allergies occur when the immune system overreacts to specific foods, such as eggs, peanuts, or milk, triggering an exaggerated immune response. Symptoms of Food Allergy Symptoms of a food allergy typically appear within two hours of consuming the offending food, though in rare cases, they may develop several hours later. If symptoms occur shortly after eating a specific food, it may indicate a food allergy. Key symptoms include hives, hoarseness, and wheezing. Additional symptoms may include: Abdominal pain Diarrhea Difficulty swallowing Itching in the mouth, throat, eyes, skin, or other areas Lightheadedness or fainting Nasal congestion Nausea Runny nose Itchy, scaly skin patches (atopic dermatitis), which may peel or blister Swelling (angioedema), especially of the eyelids, face, lips, and tongue Shortness of breath Stomach cramps Vomiting Symptoms of oral allergy syndrome may include: Itchy lips, tongue, and throat Swollen lips (occasionally) Causes of Food Allergy The immune system typically protects the body from harmful substances like bacteria, viruses, and toxins. However, in some individuals, the immune system mistakenly reacts to a harmless substance, such as a specific food. Food allergies are caused by the production of immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies in response to a particular food. This immune response leads to the release of histamine and other chemicals, causing allergic symptoms. While food intolerances are more common, true food allergies are less frequent. Any food can potentially cause an allergic reaction, but certain foods are more commonly implicated. In children, the most common food allergens include: Eggs Milk Peanuts Shellfish (e.g., shrimp, crab, lobster) Soy Tree nuts Wheat Food allergies often begin in childhood but can develop at any age. Many children outgrow allergies to milk, eggs, wheat, and soy by the age of five if these foods are avoided during early childhood. However, allergies to peanuts, tree nuts, and shellfish are usually lifelong. In older children and adults, the most common food allergens include: Fish Peanuts Shellfish Tree nuts Rarely, food additives such as dyes, thickeners, and preservatives may cause allergic or intolerance reactions. Additionally, oral allergy syndrome may occur after consuming certain fresh fruits and vegetables that contain substances similar to specific pollens. For example, melons contain compounds similar to ragweed pollen, and apples have allergens similar to tree pollen. Although many people believe they have food allergies, fewer than 1% of individuals have true food allergies. Most symptoms are due to food intolerances, such as those to: Corn products Cow's milk and dairy products Wheat and other gluten-containing grains When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Call emergency services (e.g., 911) if you experience severe or systemic reactions, such as wheezing or difficulty breathing, after eating a food. If your doctor has prescribed epinephrine for severe reactions, administer it immediately, even before calling 911. Early administration of epinephrine is critical. Anyone who has experienced an allergic reaction to food should be evaluated by an allergy specialist. Diagnosis In severe allergic reactions, symptoms may include low blood pressure and airway obstruction. Blood or skin tests may be used to confirm a food allergy, but there are no universally accepted criteria for diagnosis. Elimination diets involve avoiding suspected foods until symptoms resolve, followed by reintroducing the foods to observe for allergic reactions. Provocation (challenge) testing involves consuming small amounts of the suspected allergen under medical supervision. This test carries a risk of severe allergic reactions and should only be performed by a healthcare provider. Never attempt to provoke a reaction or reintroduce a food on your own. Treatment Options The only proven treatment for food allergies is strict avoidance of the offending food. Other treatments, such as allergy shots and probiotics, have not been definitively shown to help with food allergies. If a child has a problem with cow’s milk formula, a healthcare provider may recommend switching to a soy-based formula or an elemental formula, if available. If you suspect a food allergy in yourself or your child, consult an allergy specialist. For mild, localized symptoms (e.g., a hive on the chin after eating a specific food), treatment may not be necessary, as symptoms often resolve quickly. Antihistamines can alleviate discomfort, and soothing skin creams may provide relief. However, consult your doctor if you suspect an allergic reaction, even if it is localized. Anyone diagnosed with a food allergy should carry injectable epinephrine at all times and know how to use it. If you experience any serious or systemic reaction (even hives) after consuming the offending food, administer epinephrine and seek immediate medical attention, preferably by ambulance. Outlook and Prognosis Avoiding the offending food is often straightforward if the food is uncommon or easily identifiable. However, it may require significant dietary restrictions, careful reading of ingredient labels, and asking detailed questions when eating away from home. Possible Complications Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction that affects the entire body. Although individuals with oral allergy syndrome rarely experience anaphylaxis, they should consult their doctor to determine whether they need to carry injectable epinephrine. Food allergies can also exacerbate asthma, eczema, or other conditions. Prevention Breastfeeding may help reduce the risk of developing allergies. Otherwise, there is no known way to prevent food allergies, except by delaying the introduction of allergenic foods to infants until their gastrointestinal tract matures. The timing for this varies depending on the food and the individual child. Once an allergy develops, strict avoidance of the offending food is the best way to prevent further reactions.
